lead: Public key cryptography lets two strangers share a secret or sign a document without ever meeting. This unit shows how that is possible, from trapdoor one-way functions up to RSA, Diffie–Hellman, ElGamal, certificates, hashes, HMAC, digital signatures and zero-knowledge proofs. After it you can work a small RSA or ElGamal example by hand, explain why a browser trusts a certificate chain, and state exactly what a hash, a MAC and a signature each do and do not guarantee.
about: This unit moves from secret-key ciphers to key pairs. Chapter 4.1 states what a trapdoor one-way function is; 4.2 (RSA), 4.3 (Diffie–Hellman) and 4.4 (ElGamal) build working schemes on that idea. Chapter 4.5 shows how public keys get trusted names through certificates. The second half is about integrity: 4.6 explains hash functions and SHA, 4.7 turns a hash into a keyed MAC (HMAC), and 4.8 uses both to build digital signatures. Chapter 4.9 closes with zero-knowledge proofs, which only a few universities teach. Every chapter reuses modular arithmetic from Unit 2 and block-cipher ideas from Unit 3; protocols such as TLS, IPsec and Kerberos are handed over to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A public key system works because one function is easy to compute but practically impossible to reverse unless you hold a secret trapdoor.
chapters.depth: Define a one-way function (easy forward, infeasible backward) and a trapdoor one-way function (infeasible backward until secret information is supplied). List the five standard requirements of a public key system: cheap to generate a key pair, cheap to encrypt, cheap to decrypt, infeasible to derive the private key from the public key, and either key usable for one direction. Show the two directions: encrypt with public key gives confidentiality, encrypt with private key gives authentication. Compare with symmetric ciphers from Unit 3 on key count, speed and key size (AES-128 vs RSA-2048). Mention hybrid encryption: public key carries a session key, symmetric cipher carries the data. Some syllabi call this asymmetric key cryptography; a trapdoor one-way function is also called a trapdoor permutation when it is a bijection. State that RSA, ElGamal, Rabin and elliptic-curve schemes are all instances of this one pattern; do not derive any of them here.

figure.aria: A message passes through an easy public function; reversing it is infeasible without the trapdoor and fast with it.

chapters.example: A firm has 12 employees who must all talk privately. Symmetric keys needed: 12×11÷2 = 66. Public key pairs needed: 12, that is 12 public and 12 private keys. Now the trapdoor idea with small numbers: n = 55 and f(x) = x³ mod 55. Compute f(9) = 729 mod 55 = 14, one multiplication and one division. Going back from 14 to 9 needs the factors 5 and 11 of 55; they give φ(55) = 40 and the inverse d = 27 of e = 3, and 14²⁷ mod 55 = 9. Without the factors, the reverse step is the hard direction.
chapters.trap: Do not say the public key must be kept secret, and do not say that encrypting with the private key gives confidentiality. Two more slips: public key cryptography does not replace symmetric ciphers (it only carries the session key), and a one-way function has no trapdoor by definition, so it cannot decrypt anything.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 for modular arithmetic, exponents and Euler's theorem; Unit 3 for what a symmetric cipher and a session key are.
chapters.leave: The actual arithmetic of RSA to 4.2, Diffie–Hellman to 4.3, the question of trusting a public key to 4.5, and hybrid use inside TLS to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: RSA hides a message by raising it to a public power modulo n, and the private exponent undoes it because only the key owner knows the two primes behind n.
chapters.depth: Cover the full key generation recipe: pick large primes p and q, set n = pq and φ(n) = (p−1)(q−1), choose e with gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1, compute d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n) with the extended Euclidean algorithm. State encryption c = mᵉ mod n and decryption m = c^d mod n, and prove correctness in two lines from Euler's theorem with the case gcd(m, n) ≠ 1 handled by the Chinese remainder theorem. Give the working rule: ed ≡ 1 mod φ(n), and note the weaker sufficient condition ed ≡ 1 mod λ(n) is used in practice. Security rests on factoring n; give current sizes (2048 bits for new keys, 3072 for long life) and say factoring a 2048-bit modulus is out of reach. Name the classic attacks in one line each: common modulus, small e with small m, low private exponent (Wiener), timing, and chosen-ciphertext attacks that need padding such as OAEP. Mention Rabin's variant (security equal to factoring, four possible roots) only if your syllabus lists it. Show that textbook RSA is multiplicative, which is exactly what makes padding necessary. Do not re-teach the Euclidean algorithm.

figure.aria: Key generation produces the public pair e and n and the private d; encryption uses e and n, decryption uses d, which also appears during key generation.

chapters.example: Take p = 5, q = 11. Then n = 55 and φ(n) = 4×10 = 40. Choose e = 3, which is coprime to 40. Find d: 3×27 = 81 = 2×40 + 1, so d = 27. Encrypt m = 9: c = 9³ mod 55 = 729 mod 55 = 14. Decrypt: m = 14²⁷ mod 55. Check by the Chinese remainder theorem: mod 5, 14 ≡ 4 and 4²⁷ ≡ 4³ ≡ 4; mod 11, 14 ≡ 3 and 3²⁷ ≡ 3⁷ ≡ 9. The unique value below 55 that is 4 mod 5 and 9 mod 11 is 9, so the message returns.
chapters.trap: The most common error is writing φ(n) = pq − 1 instead of (p−1)(q−1). Others: forgetting that m must be smaller than n, claiming d is the only possible private exponent, and presenting textbook RSA as secure when it is malleable and needs OAEP padding.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the trapdoor pattern; Unit 2 for Euler's theorem, the extended Euclidean algorithm and the Chinese remainder theorem.
chapters.leave: RSA signatures to 4.8, distribution of the public key to 4.5, and practical TLS record encryption to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Two parties who share nothing can still agree on one number by each sending a public value and mixing in their own secret, because discrete logarithms are hard.
chapters.depth: Give the protocol as five steps with the public parameters p (a large prime) and g (a generator of the multiplicative group mod p, sometimes called a primitive root). State the discrete logarithm problem: given g, p and gᵃ mod p, find a. Show why both sides reach the same value g^(ab) mod p. Cover parameter choices: safe prime p = 2q + 1, a generator of the subgroup of order q, and why small-subgroup attacks are avoided. Emphasise that the output is a shared secret, not a key: both sides run it through a key derivation function and never use the raw value. Cover the man-in-the-middle weakness of the plain protocol and say that authentication, or an authenticated variant such as station-to-station, is what fixes it. Mention elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman (ECDH) in one line as the same idea over a smaller group. Do not prove the hardness of discrete log.

figure.aria: Alice sends A = 8 and Bob sends B = 19 over the public channel; each raises the other's value to their own secret and both land on the shared value 2.

chapters.example: Public parameters p = 23 and g = 5. Alice's secret a = 6, so A = 5⁶ mod 23 = 15625 mod 23 = 8. Bob's secret b = 15, so B = 5¹⁵ mod 23 = 19. Alice computes K = 19⁶ mod 23; 19² ≡ 16 and 19⁴ ≡ 3, so 19⁶ ≡ 3×16 = 48 ≡ 2. Bob computes K = 8¹⁵ mod 23; 8² ≡ 18, 8⁴ ≡ 2, 8⁸ ≡ 4, so 8¹⁵ ≡ 4×2×18×8 ≡ 2. Both hold K = 2. An eavesdropper sees 5, 23, 8, 19 and must solve 5ᵃ ≡ 8 mod 23 to get a: with p = 23 that is a short search, which is why real p has hundreds of digits.
chapters.trap: Students write that Diffie–Hellman encrypts a message, or that it authenticates the parties. It does neither. Also remember that a and b are never sent, that the shared value needs a key derivation step, and that the raw protocol falls to a man-in-the-middle.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for the one-way idea; Unit 2 for modular exponentiation, generators and the structure of the group mod p.
chapters.leave: The full man-in-the-middle attack to Unit 1, the authenticated handshake in TLS to Unit 5, and certificate-based prevention to 4.5.

chapters.idea: ElGamal turns the Diffie–Hellman exchange into an encryption scheme whose ciphertext is a pair, a fresh random power of g and the message masked by the shared value.
chapters.depth: Cover key generation (p, generator g, private x, public y = g^x mod p), encryption with a random k giving C1 = g^k mod p and C2 = m·y^k mod p, and decryption m = C2·(C1^x)⁻¹ mod p. Prove correctness in two lines. Stress that k must be fresh and secret for every message: reusing k, or leaking it, exposes the message, and a reused k across two messages leaks their ratio. Note the cost: the ciphertext is twice the message length, so ElGamal is used for keys and short data, never bulk data. Show the multiplicative property (product of ciphertexts decrypts to the product of messages) and say this is why padding or a hybrid scheme is used. Add three lines on the ElGamal signature scheme, which is a different construction from the same author, and hand the signature details to 4.8. Compare with RSA: randomised rather than deterministic, no padding needed for basic security against chosen plaintext, slower and larger.

figure.aria: Key generation makes the public y; encryption draws a random k and outputs two numbers C1 and C2; decryption rebuilds the mask from C1 and the private x.

chapters.example: Parameters p = 23, g = 5. Private key x = 6, so y = 5⁶ mod 23 = 8. Encrypt m = 7 with k = 15: C1 = 5¹⁵ mod 23 = 19, and the mask is y^k = 8¹⁵ mod 23 = 2, so C2 = 7×2 mod 23 = 14. The ciphertext is (19, 14). Decrypt: s = C1^x = 19⁶ mod 23 = 2. The inverse of 2 mod 23 is 12 because 2×12 = 24 ≡ 1. Then m = 14×12 mod 23 = 168 mod 23 = 7, the original message.
chapters.trap: The usual mistakes are to drop C1 during decryption, to reuse k for two messages (which leaks the plaintext), and to treat (C1, C2) as if C2 alone were the ciphertext. Also do not claim ElGamal gives signatures here; that is a separate scheme seen in 4.8.
chapters.prereq: 4.3 for the Diffie–Hellman mask, 4.1 for the one-way idea, and Unit 2 for modular inverses and exponentiation.
chapters.leave: ElGamal signatures and DSA to 4.8, parameter generation for large groups to a later course, and hybrid use to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A public key is useless unless you can prove it belongs to the person named, so certificates bind a name to a key with a signature from a trusted authority.
chapters.depth: List the four ways of distributing public keys: public announcement, a public directory, a key authority, and certificates; say what fails in each of the first three (forgery, tampering, single point of trust) so that certificates look necessary. Explain a certificate as a signed record: version, serial number, issuer, subject, validity dates, subject public key, extensions, and the CA's signature over all of it. Cover the X.509 standard, the CA hierarchy and the chain a browser checks from a root in its trust store down to the server certificate, revocation by CRL and by OCSP, and certificate pinning in one line. Compare a certificate based system (PKI) with a key distribution centre such as Kerberos: PKI gives non-repudiation, a KDC does not, but a KDC is online. Cover session keys and why a long-term key signs but a short-term key encrypts. Mention the web of trust briefly as an alternative trust model. Keep the mathematics out; this chapter is about trust, not arithmetic.

figure.aria: A root certificate signs an intermediate CA, which signs the bank and shop certificates; the root also signs one website certificate directly.

chapters.example: A browser connects to a fictional site bank.example and receives a chain of three certificates. It starts at the root, whose public key is already in its store with e = 3 and n = 55. The intermediate certificate carries the hash h = 9 signed as s = 4. The browser checks 4³ mod 55 = 9, so the intermediate really is signed by the root. It then repeats the check with the intermediate's key on the bank certificate, and compares the subject name with the host it typed. Now the attack: a fake certificate claiming to be bank.example carries the attacker's key and a signature made with the attacker's own key. The first verification already fails, because the attacker cannot produce a value that verifies under the root key.
chapters.trap: Say clearly that a certificate holds a public key, never the private key, and that it does not encrypt anything. Do not confuse the CA's signature on the certificate with the site owner's signature on data. Do not ignore expiry dates and revocation, which are the two ways a once-valid certificate stops being trusted.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 and 4.2 for what a key pair is and how a signature is checked; 4.8 for the checking step in detail.
chapters.leave: The TLS handshake and Kerberos tickets to Unit 5, and password and multi-factor login to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A hash function squeezes any long message into a short fixed digest, and it is built so that changing the message changes the digest in an unpredictable way.
chapters.depth: Define a cryptographic hash H: {0,1}* → {0,1}ⁿ and give the three properties: preimage resistance, second preimage resistance, collision resistance, with the implication chain between them and the brute-force cost of each (2ⁿ, 2ⁿ, 2^(n/2)). Explain the birthday bound and why it halves the effective security. Describe the Merkle–Damgård construction (pad, split into blocks, compress with a chaining value, final block gives the digest) and mention the sponge construction of SHA-3 in one line. List the families with digest sizes: MD5 (128, broken), SHA-1 (160, broken for collisions), SHA-2 with SHA-256 and SHA-512, SHA-3. List the applications: file integrity, password storage with a salt, hash-then-sign, MAC building, hash tables and deduplication, proof of work. Mention the length extension weakness of Merkle–Damgård hashes and say HMAC in 4.7 avoids it. Some syllabi call these one-way hash functions or message digests; a hash used to check data is also called a fingerprint.

figure.aria: The message is split into fixed blocks; each block is compressed with the running chaining value, and the last chaining value is the digest.

chapters.example: A toy iterated hash with 4-bit values: hᵢ = (hᵢ₋₁ + Bᵢ) mod 16, starting from h₀ = 2. Message blocks 3, 7, 5 give h = 2+3 = 5, then 5+7 = 12, then 12+5 = 17 mod 16 = 1. Digest: 1. Change the last block to 6: the digest becomes 2. Now a collision: blocks 4, 6, 5 give 6, then 12, then 1, the same digest 1. This toy is trivially breakable because it only adds, so it has none of the three properties. Real compression functions mix and shift so that a collision costs about 2^(n/2) work: a 256-bit digest needs about 2¹²⁸ hashes by the birthday attack, which is out of reach.
chapters.trap: Do not call hashing encryption: there is no key and no way back. Do not say collision resistance costs 2ⁿ operations; the birthday attack makes it 2^(n/2). Also distinguish the three properties, because a question often asks which property a given attack breaks.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for block-by-block processing of data, and basic probability for the birthday bound.
chapters.leave: Keyed hashing and HMAC to 4.7, hash-then-sign to 4.8, and password hashing policy to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A MAC uses a shared secret key over a message so the receiver knows the message came from someone holding the key and was not altered, without encrypting anything.
chapters.depth: Define a MAC as a pair (tag generation, verification) with a shared key, and state what it gives (integrity, message authentication, replay protection when a nonce or sequence number is included) and what it does not give (confidentiality, non-repudiation, since both sides hold the key). Contrast with a plain hash (no key, anyone can compute) and with a digital signature (no shared secret, gives non-repudiation). Cover CBC-MAC and its requirement of fixed-length input, then HMAC in full: tag = H((K ⊕ opad) ‖ H((K ⊕ ipad) ‖ M)), with ipad = 0x36 and opad = 0x5C repeated to the block size. Explain why H(K ‖ M) is unsafe under Merkle–Damgård: length extension lets an attacker append data. Cover key length, truncation, and the rule that a MAC must be verified in constant time. Explain the CCA motivation from Unit 3: MAC-then-encrypt, encrypt-then-MAC (preferred) and encrypt-and-MAC, and name AEAD modes such as GCM in one line.

figure.aria: The key is mixed with the inner pad and hashed with the message, then mixed with the outer pad and hashed again to give the tag.

chapters.example: Use the toy hash hᵢ = (hᵢ₋₁ + Xᵢ) mod 16 from 4.6, with 4-bit stand-ins for the pads: key K = 5, ipad = 6, opad = 12. Inner: K ⊕ ipad = 3, so H(3 ‖ 7 ‖ 4) runs 0+3 = 3, 3+7 = 10, 10+4 = 14. Outer: K ⊕ opad = 9, so H(9 ‖ 14) runs 0+9 = 9, 9+14 = 23 mod 16 = 7. The tag is 7. Compare the naive H(K ‖ M) = H(5 ‖ 7 ‖ 4), which gives 5, 12, then 16 mod 16 = 0. A receiver who sees message blocks 7, 4 and tag 0 cannot tell whether block 5 was the key or part of the message, and in a real Merkle–Damgård hash the attacker could extend the message and still predict the new tag. The two-layer HMAC computation hides the inner state from that attack.
chapters.trap: A MAC gives no confidentiality and no non-repudiation, because both sides hold the key; do not mix those up with a digital signature. Do not accept H(K ‖ M) as a MAC, and do not ignore the order of encryption and MAC in a combined scheme.
chapters.prereq: 4.6 for hash properties and the Merkle–Damgård structure; Unit 3 for CBC mode, CCA security and block ciphers.
chapters.leave: AEAD records inside TLS and IPsec to Unit 5, and signatures to 4.8.

chapters.idea: A digital signature is the private-key operation on a hash of the message, so anyone can check it with the public key while only the key owner could have produced it.
chapters.depth: List what a signature must give: message authentication, integrity, non-repudiation, and unforgeability even against an attacker who can ask for signatures on chosen messages. Show the general recipe: hash the message, then apply the private key to the digest. Work RSA signatures fully: s = h^d mod n and the check h = s^e mod n, with PKCS#1 v1.5 or PSS padding. Explain why hashing first is needed: RSA can only sign values below n, and hashing binds the whole message in one step. Show textbook RSA forgery by multiplicativity as the reason padding is mandatory. Cover existential versus universal forgery in one line each. Name DSA, ECDSA and the ElGamal signature scheme as alternatives with their own verification equations, without full derivations unless the syllabus asks. Add one line each on blind signatures, timestamping and code signing as applications. Mention that a signature does not hide the message.

figure.aria: The signer hashes the message and raises the digest to the private exponent; the verifier hashes the received message and raises the signature to the public exponent, then compares.

chapters.example: Keys from 4.2: p = 5, q = 11, n = 55, e = 3, d = 27. Let the message hash be h = 9. The signature is s = 9²⁷ mod 55. Working mod 5 and mod 11, both give 4, so s = 4. The verifier computes 4³ mod 55 = 64 mod 55 = 9 and accepts. Now the forgery: suppose the scheme signs raw values and the attacker already holds the valid pair (9, 4) and another valid pair (4, 49), since 49³ mod 55 = 4. Multiply: 9×4 mod 55 = 36 and 4×49 mod 55 = 196 mod 55 = 31. Check 31³ mod 55 = 29791 mod 55 = 36. So 31 is a valid signature on 36, produced without d. Padding stops this, because the padded hash of a real message is never the product of two other padded hashes.
chapters.trap: Do not sign the raw message instead of the hash, and do not claim that signing with the private key keeps the message secret. Do not say a signature gives confidentiality. Also be careful with the words: encrypting with the private key is not the definition, it is a coincidence of textbook RSA.
chapters.prereq: 4.2 for RSA exponents, 4.6 for hash properties; 4.5 for how the verifier trusts the public key.
chapters.leave: Certificate chains to 4.5, and signed protocols such as TLS, Kerberos and S/MIME to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A zero-knowledge proof convinces the verifier that a statement is true while revealing nothing except its truth.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic; keep it to the interface and one protocol. Give the three properties: completeness (an honest prover always convinces), soundness (a cheating prover fails except with small probability), and zero knowledge (the verifier learns nothing beyond the truth, formally that a simulator could produce the transcript alone). Define honest-verifier zero knowledge, the weaker notion most courses state. Present one protocol fully: 3-colouring of a graph. The prover commits to a random permutation of a valid colouring, the verifier challenges one edge, the prover opens the two endpoint colours, and the verifier checks that they differ; repeat for many rounds. Show that a wrong colouring passes with probability at most (1 − 1/|E|) per round and that revealing one edge each round leaks nothing. Mention graph isomorphism and Schnorr as other examples, the Fiat–Shamir transform for making the proof non-interactive, and commitments built from hashes. Name the uses: password-free login, privacy in blockchain, and proofs of correctness in cloud computing.

figure.aria: The prover commits to hidden colours, the verifier challenges one edge, the prover opens only the two endpoint colours, and the verifier accepts when they differ; the rounds repeat.

chapters.example: The statement is: this triangle graph has a 3-colouring, and I know one. The prover permutes the colours at random in each round and commits to one hidden colour per vertex. The verifier names one of the 3 edges at random. For an honest prover with colours 1, 2, 3 the two endpoints always differ, so it passes every round. A cheating prover with only two colours must give the triangle two vertices of the same colour, so exactly one of the 3 edges is monochromatic and it passes with probability 2/3 per round, not 1/3. After 10 independent rounds the chance of passing every time is (2/3)¹⁰ ≈ 0.017, under 2 percent. Nothing about the full colouring leaks, because each round opens one edge under a fresh random permutation.
chapters.trap: Do not say zero knowledge means the verifier learns nothing at all; the verifier does learn that the statement is true. Do not swap soundness and completeness, and do not forget that the prover must reshuffle and recommit every round, since reusing one commitment lets the verifier collect many edges and rebuild the colouring.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for one-way functions, 4.6 for the hash commitments used to hide colours; a little probability for the soundness error.
chapters.leave: NP-completeness and reductions to a theory course, and blockchain and cryptocurrency to Unit 6.
